title: Identifiability-aware neural ordinary differential equations for parsimonious and reliable dynamic modelling

content.abstract_summary: Proposes iNODE (identifiability-aware neural ODE), a framework that embeds structural and practical identifiability diagnostics directly into the neural ODE architecture selection and training process. Uses the Model Quality Ranking Index (MQRI) — a composite score combining Fisher Information Matrix-based identifiability, prediction confidence intervals, and validation error — to select parsimonious architectures. Demonstrates on four pharmacological benchmarks that iNODE produces models 20–50× smaller than conventional NODEs while achieving 3–6× lower validation errors and reducing maximum parameter confidence intervals from 881% to 84%.
key_findings: iNODE integrates structural identifiability analysis (via symbolic tools) and practical identifiability (Fisher Information Matrix + profile likelihood) directly into architecture search, not as a post-hoc check

Model Quality Ranking Index (MQRI) is a composite metric weighting identifiability, parameter confidence intervals, and held-out validation error — enables systematic model selection across architectures without manual tuning
Benchmark 1 (PK/PD system): iNODE achieved 32 parameters vs. 1,362 in conventional NODE (42× smaller), with 3× lower validation error and dramatically tighter CIs

Benchmark results across 4 pharmacological case studies: maximum parameter CI reduced from 881% to 84% (representative benchmark) — non-identifiable conventional NODE parameters rendered practically useless for dose optimization or simulation

Architecture selection: iNODE prunes network width and depth based on identifiability metrics, converging on sparse architectures that are interpretable and reliably estimated from clinical trial-sized datasets

The iNODE framework is directly applicable to hybrid mechanistic-ML models (NLME context) where the mechanistic compartments are known but ML augmentation modules are unconstrained — a gap the MCS WG has identified for Pillar 1
Submitted August 13, 2026 — very recent preprint, not yet peer-reviewed; findings need independent replication across more complex model structures
limitations: Preprint — not yet peer-reviewed; identifiability claims need independent replication
Benchmarks are pharmacological but may not capture the full complexity of NLME population models with inter-individual variability (IIV) — a critical dimension for PMx applications
MQRI weights (identifiability vs. validation error vs. CI width) are heuristically set — sensitivity of architecture selection to these weights is not fully characterized

Symbolic structural identifiability analysis does not scale well to very high-dimensional systems (e.g., QSP-scale models with 100+ ODEs); the practical scope is compartmental-to-moderate hybrid models
The 4 benchmarks are described as 'pharmacological' but case study specifics (drug, disease, data source) not fully detailed in the arXiv abstract — full-text read needed

extracted_claims.text: iNODE produces architectures 20–50× smaller than conventional NODE while achieving 3–6× lower validation errors
Maximum parameter confidence intervals reduced from 881% to 84% — non-identifiable conventional NODE parameters are practically useless for downstream inference and decision-making
Identifiability analysis integrated as an architectural constraint, not a post-hoc diagnostic — this is the key methodological departure from prior neural ODE work

Architecture size reduction: iNODE vs. conventional NODE across benchmarks

gaps_addressed: Directly fills the WG's Pillar 1 gap: the field lacks systematic methods to ensure neural ODE components in hybrid models are identifiable from clinical data — iNODE proposes the first architecture-level solution

MQRI provides a concrete model selection criterion for hybrid models that incorporates identifiability alongside predictive performance — exactly what M1.2 (structural identifiability of neural ODE components) and M1.4 (when do hybrids help?) need
Pillar 2 (UQ): the CI reduction results (881%→84%) quantify the practical cost of ignoring identifiability in UQ — a compelling motivating example for the WG's uncertainty quantification workstream
The 20–50× parameter reduction has regulatory implications — smaller, identifiable models are easier to inspect and validate under FDA's credibility assessment framework
